title: Previews that stress the key concepts
statement: A preview given before new material helps when it stresses the key concepts, not only their structure.
example: In two experiments, with 48 and 53 students, well-structured organisers raised far transfer from roughly 33% to 67%, yet structure on its own was not reliably better.
detail: An intro-video BrainLift for a Grade 3 reading course reports Gurlitt, Dummel, Schuster and Nückles (2012): in two experiments, with 48 psychology and 53 mathematics students, well-structured advance organisers beat less-structured ones on the schemata learners formed, the posttest, and near and far transfer, with far transfer rising from roughly 33% to 67% (`downloads/BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md`, line 456). A well-structured organiser on its own was not reliably better (p = .10 in the first experiment, and no far-transfer gain in the second); what carried it was the version that also emphasised the key concepts. The source names the study without a link; its DOI was found on Crossref.
against: One study, with psychology and mathematics students rather than young readers.

evidence.path: BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md
evidence.quote: What carried it was the version that additionally emphasised the key concepts. Structure without emphasis was not enough.
Spec §3.3 cites Stone (1983) directly for the linked advance-organizer video: "modest but reliable gains, strongest for long-term retention."
They give modest but reliable gains, strongest for long-term retention (Stone, 1983).
